How Marketing Services Are Priced: Five Fee Models

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 20 April 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

Marketing services are priced five ways: retainer, project fee, hourly or daily, percent of spend, and performance. Each rewards the provider for something different, so find what makes the fee go up and you have found the advice you will get. The market is moving: a 2026 study of 69 multinational advertisers found fewer than a fifth now pay agencies mainly for time, and 61% plan to change their commercial models because of AI. Yet only 45% said they had enough visibility into how agencies cost and profit from the work.

The fee structure in a marketing proposal is the most reliable predictor of the advice you will receive. Five models cover almost every arrangement, and each one pays the provider for a different thing.

The five models

Retainer. A fixed monthly fee for an ongoing scope of work. Rewards the provider for keeping the relationship. Good for continuous work, running programmes, managing channels, producing a regular cadence of content, and for predictability on both sides. The risk is scope drift: the work quietly shrinks while the fee does not, or expands while the fee does not, depending on who is paying less attention.

Project fee. A fixed price for a defined deliverable with a defined end. Rewards the provider for finishing. Good for work with a clear scope: a diagnostic, a positioning exercise, a programme built and handed over, a launch. The risk is the scope document: a vague one produces disputes about what "done" meant.

Hourly or daily. Payment for time. Rewards the provider for spending time. Good for truly unpredictable work where neither side can scope in advance, and for very short engagements. The risk is obvious: the model pays for slowness, and the client carries all the estimation risk.

Percent of spend. A fee calculated as a share of the media budget the provider manages. Rewards the provider for spending more. The historical standard for media agencies and the model with the sharpest conflict of interest: every recommendation about budget, channel, and pace is made by a party paid more when the answer is "more."

Performance. Payment tied to outcomes: leads, customers, revenue, or a bonus above a threshold. Rewards the provider for results, in principle. In practice it depends entirely on how the outcome is defined, measured, and attributed, and on who controls the measurement. Pure performance deals also push the provider toward the easiest outcomes and away from anything slow, such as brand, content, or a channel that takes a quarter to work.

What the market data shows

The ANA's 18th Trends in Agency Compensation survey, published in December 2022, covered 101 US marketers and 336 agency relationships. It found 82% used fee-based compensation, up from 68% in 2016, and that labour-based fees, essentially paying for agency time, remained dominant, at 76% among smaller advertisers. Fixed or output-based fees had risen sharply among the largest spenders.

Outside the US the move away from time is further along. The World Federation of Advertisers and Agency Mania Solutions surveyed 69 multinationals with a combined $147 billion in marketing spend; trade press reported the results in September and October 2026. Labour-based pay as the main model had fallen from 54% of companies in 2011 to under a fifth. Fixed-fee and output models had grown to about a third. AI is a stated reason: agencies can now produce more in less time, which makes paying by the hour harder to defend. Only 20% of respondents had already changed their commercial model in response to AI, and 61% intended to.

Performance pay is talked about more than it is used. In the ANA data, 41% of advertisers used performance incentives in 2022, down from 48% in 2016 and 61% in 2013, and most said they did not know whether incentives improved agency performance. In the WFA study, performance pay made up less than 20% of total agency compensation for most respondents, and financial incentives scored 3.9 out of 6 as a driver of agency performance, against 5.6 for a good brief. Our piece Performance marketing is not a channel, it is a way of paying makes the same point from the buyer's side.

Find the fee. Ask what makes it go up. That is what the provider is being paid to do.

What to read in a proposal

Find the fee. Ask what makes it go up. That is what the provider is being paid to do.

A retainer goes up when the relationship lasts. A project fee does not go up at all, which is why providers who quote them care about scope. Hourly goes up with time. Percent of spend goes up with budget. Performance goes up with outcomes as defined in the contract, so read the definition.

Then ask what is not included. Every model has edges, and the profitable part of many engagements is the work that falls outside the original description.

Percent of spend deserves a second read, because what the provider earns may not all appear on the invoice. The ANA's 2016 investigation by K2 Intelligence found US media agencies receiving cash rebates and free inventory based on client spend, and buying media as principals for resale to clients at mark-ups of roughly 30% to 90%. Advertisers interviewed were often unaware of the rebates. The WFA's 2026 finding that only 45% of multinationals have enough visibility into agency costing suggests the gap has not closed. Our piece Percent of spend is a conflict of interest with a logo on it makes the wider case.

The combination that tends to work

For most companies buying distribution work, the least conflicted structure is a project fee against a written scope for anything with an end, a flat retainer for anything ongoing, media fees stated in dollars per account rather than as a percentage, no provider fronting the media spend, and a performance component only where the outcome is defined in writing and measured in the client's own systems.

That is the structure we publish, and we publish it because the alternative, a menu of fee models chosen to suit each deal, leaves the client guessing what the advice is for.

The same logic runs through services pricing generally. A price should be anchored to the value of the outcome and stated before the work starts, which is the argument of our pieces on pricing architecture for services firms and value-based pricing. Where AI products now charge per outcome, the same definitional discipline applies; see outcome-based pricing for AI.

Two rules for the buyer

Never accept a free proposal for anything past a short conversation. A free proposal is a sales document, and the provider's cost of producing it is recovered somewhere in the engagement. The European Association of Communications Agencies put the average agency cost of a new-business pitch at about €43,800 in 2025. That money comes back in later fees. A paid, scoped first step, priced low enough to be an easy decision, produces advice with a defined end and no obligation.

And insist that the next step be priced in the same proposal as the current one. A provider who will not say what the next engagement costs until the current one is finished is pricing on dependency.

Retainers pay for relationships, project fees for finishing, hourly for time, percent of spend for spending, and performance for outcomes as defined. Find what makes the fee go up, and you have found the advice you will get.

lowob takeaways

  • Read the fee for the incentive. Each model pays for a different behaviour, and the advice follows the pay.
  • Treat percent of spend with care. State media fees in dollars and secure audit rights.
  • Define performance in writing. Measure it in your own systems, or do not pay on it.
  • Price the next step now. A provider who will not is pricing on dependency.

Common questions

What are the main ways marketing agencies charge?

Five models cover almost every arrangement: a monthly retainer, a fixed project fee, hourly or daily rates, a percent of media spend, and performance-based fees tied to outcomes.

Is percent-of-spend agency pricing a conflict of interest?

It is the model with the sharpest conflict: every recommendation about budget, channel and pace is made by a party paid more when the answer is "more." The ANA's 2016 investigation also found rebates and mark-ups clients often could not see.

Are agencies moving away from hourly billing?

Among large advertisers, yes. A 2026 WFA study found fewer than a fifth of multinationals now pay agencies mainly for time, with fixed-fee and output models at about a third, and most expect AI to speed the shift.

Should I accept a free marketing proposal?

Not for anything past a short conversation. A free proposal is a sales document whose cost is recovered somewhere in the engagement; a paid, scoped first step gives advice with a defined end.
